title: Jasper and the Tale Twister
markdown:
Wizard Jasper carefully pushed his glasses up his nose. They felt like tiny waterfalls sparkling on his face. “Alright, Pudding,” he rumbled, his voice warm as a folded blanket. Pudding, who was always so neat and tidy, was carefully washing one paw. He sat on top of a tall stack of dusty books. “The Chronicle of Echoes task at the annual Mountain Valley Festival. What a fun job. It is just a matter of telling our favourite local legends. I have already checked them against three old scrolls, asked the moss-sprites, and even got the grumpy mountain troll’s top picks. Easy peasy, right?”

Pudding blinked slowly, a look Jasper knew well. It meant something like: as long as there is a sunbeam and a warm spot for a nap later, I guess I can put up with your excitement, Master.

The Mountain Valley Festival was always a happy noisy colourful blast. Bright banners fluttered in the fresh mountain air. The air smelled of roasted pine nuts and spiced apple cider. Jasper, holding his special storybook, stood before a small crowd near the entrance to the famous Cave Libraries. He cleared his throat, making a little show of it. He was ready to tell the legendary tale of the Sunstone Serpent.

“Long ago, when mountains sang and rivers whispered secrets,” he began, his voice warm and practised, “a magnificent Serpent made of pure sunlight lived in the highest, hardest-to-reach peaks of our valley…”

“Actually,” a clear gentle voice cut in, sounding like tiny silver bells. “If I may say so, it was not pure sunlight. The old scrolls, especially the Codex of Glacial Whispers, said it was lumina compressa. That meant it was like light from a squeezed-together dawn. And the Serpent, while magnificent, was more like a grand, almost airy creature than just a regular animal.”

Jasper’s jaw almost dropped. He had worked for days on that opening sentence. He shot a worried glance at Pudding. Pudding was rubbing against his ankle, giving it a definite insistent rub. This particular rub meant: you are getting a bit worked up, Master. Take a deep breath and maybe look at an interesting dust speck for a moment. Embarrassment arrived, hot and prickly.

“Ah, yes,” Jasper managed, his voice a little tighter than he liked. “Of course. A grand creature of squeezed-together dawn light. It was coiled around the highest peaks, a shining beacon for miles and miles…”

“The texts say coiled is too active a word for its position,” Eldrin, the elf archivist, said smoothly. He stepped forward from the crowd, holding a small perfectly smooth slate that seemed to glow from within. “The Serpent was described more as being in dormant repose. And it could only be seen from the shepherd paths on very clear Tuesdays, and only during the spring equinox.”

A soft sound, like a stream tumbling over smooth stones, rippled through the crowd. Giggles. Jasper felt a blush creep up his neck, as warm and steady as summer sun. Pudding, nearby, let out a tiny silent sigh. This was becoming a masterclass in glorious, if slightly embarrassing, awkwardness. But then Jasper’s eyes sparkled with a mischievous idea. He decided to try a new, much more bendy approach.

“Ah, yes. Dormant repose, naturally,” Jasper declared, his voice suddenly regaining its sparkle. “The Serpent, in its magnificent dormant repose, was a creature of squeezed-together dawn light, shining like a beacon that, on clear Tuesdays, could indeed be spotted from the shepherd paths. And who knows,” he leaned in, his voice hushed with a playful secret, “maybe the scrolls also mentioned how it sometimes chased its own tail when it was feeling especially playful, just to liven things up?”

Eldrin paused, tilting his head. His usually calm elf face showed a flicker of surprise. His slate stayed poised, but his brow furrowed a tiny bit. “The tail-chasing… that is an interesting thought, though not written down anywhere. But,” he admitted, a tiny smile playing on his lips, “it does add a certain story flavour, does it not?”

Because Jasper bent instead of bristling, Eldrin’s corrections became steps in a dance. Jasper would say a sentence, Eldrin would offer a very precise, often funny, small correction, and Jasper would then cleverly weave that correction back into the story. Sometimes he would add a funny twist that made Eldrin himself let out a soft unexpected chuckle — a sound as rare and lovely as a star sapphire. The crowd loved it, laughing loudly and clapping with delight.

As the sky began to turn soft shades of purple, pink, and deep indigo, the festival ended with a village gathering. A big bonfire crackled cheerfully in the middle of the square. The valley lights, far below, twinkled like spilled stars. Villagers shared bowls of thick stew and slices of sweet sun-ripened berry cake. Eldrin came over as Jasper sat by the fire. He held out a small smooth grey stone.

“For your team spirit, Wizard Jasper,” he whispered, then melted back into the shadows to keep organising the day’s gathered stories. Pudding purred contentedly on Jasper’s lap, a warm rumbling sound that matched the evening.

And so the valley learned that a tale told only by the scroll sits still, but a tale shared with a friend will chase its own tail and still be true.
characters: Jasper (wizard who checks legends against three scrolls), Pudding (a cat who prefers sunbeams)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
